title: "N-gram"
description: "A contiguous sequence of n items, commonly words or characters, used to represent local context in language."
term: "N-gram"

## Simple explanation

An n-gram is a group of $n$ neighboring tokens. A one-word group is a
unigram, a two-word group is a bigram, and a three-word group is a trigram.
For example, "machine learning works" contains the bigrams "machine
learning" and "learning works."

## Technical explanation

N-grams are contiguous token sequences extracted from text. They provide a
simple way to represent local word order for language modeling, search,
classification, and feature engineering. The sequence may consist of words,
characters, or other tokens.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

N-grams are useful baselines for text classification and information
retrieval, and they help explain how language models estimate likely
continuations. They are inexpensive to compute but represent only a limited
context window.

## How it works

Given a token sequence $w_1,\ldots,w_T$, a sliding window of length $n$
produces the sequence $(w_i,\ldots,w_{i+n-1})$. A statistical n-gram language
model estimates the next token using only the preceding $n-1$ tokens:

$$
P(w_t \mid w_1,\ldots,w_{t-1})
\approx
P(w_t \mid w_{t-n+1},\ldots,w_{t-1})
$$

Sparse counts for unseen sequences are often handled with smoothing.

## Practical example

For the sentence "a small model learns," a bigram featurizer can produce
"a small," "small model," and "model learns." A spam classifier can use
these phrase features alongside individual word counts.

## Common misconceptions

- An n-gram is not necessarily a sequence of words; character n-grams are common too.
- Increasing $n$ does not always improve a model: larger sequences are sparser and need more data.
- N-grams capture local order, not long-range meaning or the full context of a sentence.
